title: Rumyana Ivanova v. Bulgaria
facts:
The applicant, Ms Rumyana Ivanova, born in 1952 and living in Sofia, was a parliamentary reporter for 24 Hours, a leading Bulgarian national daily. After the 1996-97 banking crisis, the Information on Non-Performing Credits Act of 1997 required the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) to compile a list of borrowers whose loans had been due for more than six months. The list was to be sent to the Chief Prosecutor's Office, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the tax and customs authorities and the National Assembly, and published in a special bulletin. People on the list were colloquially called 'credit millionaires'. On 21 January 1998 the list was presented to the chairman of the National Assembly.

Mr M. D. was a Member of Parliament for the Movement for Rights and Freedoms from 1994 to 1997. He was deputy chairman of the Economy Committee and a member of the Budget and Finance Committee. In 2001 he became involved with the National Movement Simeon II, which won the June 2001 elections, and he held shares in various companies. On 22 January 1998 the daily Trud reported that several companies connected with his name were on the list: Maxcom Holding (BGL 3.2 billion owed), FBK Maxcom (BGL 9.4 billion) and Maxcom OOD (BGL 7.8 billion). Mr M. D. sued Trud's publisher for libel. On 9 January 1999 the Sofia City Court dismissed the action as unsubstantiated, since he had adduced no evidence of damage.

On 3 August 2001 the National Movement Simeon II parliamentary group held a closed meeting to discuss candidates for deputy Minister of Finance in charge of customs. In the National Assembly lobby, MPs told journalists, including the applicant, that Mr M. D. was being considered. One MP said his candidacy would probably not be approved because the Prime Minister was wary that his name appeared on the 'credit millionaires' list.

The applicant took several steps before writing her article:
- She telephoned Mr N., press officer of the customs administration, who said that as far as he knew this was so. He referred her to Trud's 1998 publication 'Full list of credit millionaires', whose preface stated that FBK Maxcom and Maxcom OOD were linked to Mr M. D.
- She checked an electronic law database and found that Mr M. D. had been a member of Vitaplant OOD, directly and after 1993 through another company. That company was also on the list.
- She tried unsuccessfully to reach Mr M. D. by telephone.

According to the applicant, colleagues contacted various institutions, which confirmed that Mr M. D. was on the list.

On 4 August 2001 her article appeared on page eight under the headline 'Foreign Company to Run Customs under Concession?', with photographs of Mr M. D. and Mr E. D. It read: "The King's men were intensely discussing whether to hire a Western company to run the customs administration, Members of Parliament say. The idea became topical because of difficulties with the selection of a strong candidate for the position of deputy Minister of Finance in charge of supervising the customs administration. The proposal that Mr M. D. is tapped for the position has not yet been approved by the Prime Minister. Simeon Saxe-Coburggotski was concerned about the fact that [Mr M. D.]'s name is on the list of credit millionaires, confided sources close to him. In the official document dated 21 January 1998 and signed by the head of the Bank Supervision [department of the Bulgarian National Bank], [Ms E. M.], [Mr M. D.] appears as a debtor. Three of his companies – Maxcom Holding, FBK Maxcom and Maxcom OOD –, had debts totalling 20,400,000 levs. The uncertainties about [Mr M. D.] have brought the name of [Mr E. D.] on to the agenda. However, the idea was for him to have operational control over customs, while the concession is awarded to the Western company."

That day Mr M. D. told the applicant the statements were untrue. He also told the editor that he was not a shareholder in the three companies. The editor amended the article for subsequent copies, which carried only Mr M. D.'s photograph. The amended version read: "The King's men were discussing whether to hire a Western company to run the customs administration, Members of Parliament say. The idea became topical because of difficulties with the selection of a strong candidate for the position of deputy Minister of Finance in charge of supervising the customs administration. The proposal that Mr M. D. is tapped for the position has not yet been approved by the Prime Minister. According to insiders, Simeon Saxe-Coburggotski received reports that [Mr M. D.] is on the list of credit millionaires. In the official document dated 21 January 1998 and signed by the head of the Bank Supervision [department of the Bulgarian National Bank], [Ms E. M.], [Mr M. D.] appears as a debtor. Mr M. D. categorically denied this. He said 'I am not a debtor, but a creditor'. According to former Members of Parliament, the allegations that he was a credit millionaire were being spread by people who wanted to smear his name. Ill-wishers used the similarity between the names of [Mr M. D.]'s companies and the names of those companies featuring on the list of credit millionaires. This was done to foil his candidacy for the position of deputy Minister of Finance. In recent days the name of [Mr E. D.] has been brought on to the agenda. However, the idea was for him to have operational control over customs, while the concession is awarded to the Western company."

The first version appeared in 5,205 copies, of which 5,079 were sold. The second appeared in 230,817 copies, of which 202,568 were sold.

On 6 August 2001 the newspaper published Mr M. D.'s response under the headline '[M. D.]: I am not a credit millionaire!'. He stated that he had never been a shareholder, member or manager of the three companies, could not otherwise be linked with debtor companies, and that the newspaper had joined an orchestrated smear campaign. He later withdrew his candidacy.

On 8 October 2001 Mr M. D. lodged a private criminal complaint for libel under Articles 147 § 1 and 148 §§ 1(2) and 2 of the Criminal Code. He sought BGN 10,000, which he pledged to donate to a church. The applicant replied that she had relayed information from MPs, verified through all available sources, and that the vilifying circumstance was being a 'credit millionaire', which was true.

The Sofia District Court heard the case on five dates in 2002 and examined witnesses, including the journalist Ms N. It initially allowed, but then refused, evidence on Mr M. D.'s links with debtor companies. It permitted the applicant to call one of the MPs, but she failed to secure his attendance and refused to name him, so the court could not subpoena him.

On 16 September 2002 the District Court convicted her. Applying Article 78a, it replaced criminal liability with an administrative fine of BGN 500, the minimum. It awarded Mr M. D. BGN 2,000 in damages plus interest, and BGN 550 in costs. Its reasoning was as follows:
- 'Credit millionaire' carried a negative connotation and was vilifying.
- The smaller circulation of the first version was immaterial.
- The applicant had acted with recklessness, because she had not carried out a proper journalistic enquiry with confirmation from two independent sources.
- The MP was an unreliable off-the-record source. Mr N. merely relied on Trud's preface, which named companies rather than shareholders.
- Vitaplant OOD was not among the companies named, which should have prompted further checks.
- She could have consulted the public register of companies and had enough time to do so.
- She relied on an official BNB document she had not seen.
- As an experienced journalist she likely knew of earlier publications that had been refuted.

It mitigated the fine for her means, critical attitude, cooperation and good character, and declined occupational disqualification. It awarded only part of the damages claimed because career and business harm was unproven.

On appeal the applicant argued that she had been restricted in proving the truth of her allegations, that mens rea was lacking given the prior publications, that Article 10 had been violated, that she had relayed information from an MP acting officially, and that Mr M. D. was indeed a 'credit millionaire' through Vitaplant OOD. The Sofia City Court admitted evidence on Vitaplant OOD and found that Mr M. D. had participated in it indirectly.

In a final judgment of 19 May 2003 the Sofia City Court upheld the conviction. It reasoned as follows:
- 'Credit millionaire' was a pejorative journalistic term. No official BNB list of 'credit millionaires' existed, only a list of non-performing credits above DEM 5,000.
- The statement could not be dissected: the untrue specifics (an official document naming him and three named companies with specific debts) made the allegation persuasive, and the degree of defamation depended on those specifics.
- An individual could be deemed a 'credit millionaire' only through a direct and substantial connection with a debtor company. Mr M. D. had not participated directly in Vitaplant OOD, was not its manager or a substantial shareholder, and its credit was not of a scale to make him a 'millionaire'.
- The earlier civil judgment was irrelevant and not binding.
- Although the applicant had consulted two sources and had seen prior publications, she acted recklessly by failing to check the only reliable source, the public register of companies. She was aware that the information might be inaccurate but disregarded this in order to publish quickly.
applicantSubmissions: In a democratic society it is not necessary to resort to penal sanctions to curtail freedom of expression; criminal law has an unduly chilling effect on freedom of expression, particularly for journalists, who do not have their own sources but rely on others for information.
Criminal liability is problematic because journalists work and verify information in teams, whereas penal sanctions are individual.

Requiring defendants in defamation proceedings to prove the truth of their statements is disproportionate. The courts examine only the truth of the statements and do not examine the reputation of the person allegedly defamed, which is wrongly assumed to be good. This leads to abuse of rights and de facto no-fault liability.

The courts did not consider the extent to which the allegations actually affected Mr M. D.'s reputation. They wrongly held him defamed because of a simple mistake in the names of the companies through which he featured on the bad debtors' list.

The publication did not materially affect Mr M. D.'s standing in society. Its purpose was to inform the public about the candidates for deputy Minister of Finance, and the availability of information on that topic mattered more than the identity of the company through which he featured on the list.

The finding that the statement was untrue was erroneous. Only the names of the companies were wrong; Mr M. D. was in fact a 'credit millionaire', as shown by his participation in Vitaplant OOD. Her error was induced by the Members of Parliament who tipped her off.

The Government's claim that she did not consult the Bulgarian National Bank list conflicts with the Sofia City Court's own finding that Mr M. D. featured on that list through Vitaplant OOD, which she proved.
The Sofia City Court's ruling that she had to check the register of companies was excessive. No such obligation existed, and the check would have been unfeasible given the time it would have taken.

The domestic courts erred in not calling the Members of Parliament she had spoken to, whose names emerged from Ms N.'s testimony. These MPs, one of whom was a business associate of Mr M. D., tricked her into publishing inaccurate information in order to procure a judgment declaring that he was not a 'credit millionaire' and to conceal his involvement in Vitaplant OOD.
Mr M. D. suffered no real prejudice to his reputation, because through Vitaplant OOD he had taken out loans and failed to repay them, as shown by contracts he himself produced in court.
governmentSubmissions: Journalists' freedom of expression should not be exercised by damaging individuals' reputations. The key question is whether the journalist fulfilled her duty to ensure the accuracy of the information. Here the public was misled because the information was untrue.

Journalists relying on an official document need not verify its accuracy. However, the applicant neither consulted the official BNB list nor checked the register of companies. She trusted her sources without verification, although Trud's book and its preface were not an official publication.

The applicant failed to carry out a proper journalistic enquiry. She supported her allegation with specific but untrue statements that created a false impression of verified, authentic information, and she admitted at trial that she had not properly verified it.
The statement was negative, led to grave public disapproval of Mr M. D., and was presented as a statement of fact. It therefore required serious proof.

Both domestic courts allowed the parties to adduce evidence on the truth of the allegation and found it untrue, giving ample reasons. The Sofia City Court specifically addressed the argument concerning Mr M. D.'s participation in another company.
The remedy used by Mr M. D., a private criminal complaint with a civil claim, was ordinary and available to anyone whose reputation is attacked.
The courts waived the applicant's criminal liability and imposed only an administrative punishment, and the damages awarded were not unreasonable.
